segments.text: Vanguard
"Two apples for a copper or five for two, and don't tell me the ones at the bottom are bruised because I packed them myself. If you want unbruised apples you can come at dawn like everybody else."
- A woman at the Vanguard market
The Watchtower

Vanguard sits two days south of Brenmath on the Quiet Road, on the northern shore of Lake Verdane. Every Remosan March in living memory has come through it. In the long decades between Marches the village brews beer, grows apples, forges ironwork, and provisions the city it is sworn to warn.

About six hundred people live here in stone houses along narrow lanes. The Quiet Road widens at the center of the village into a small square with a low stone marker at its middle, carved with the first day of each of the three Marches and nothing else. People walking past will sometimes touch the marker without thinking about it. West of the village the land opens into grain fields and old apple orchards, the orchards dense and overgrown in places, crossed by paths that are not obvious to outsiders and cache-pits in the older trees that have been there for generations. South, Lake Verdane, close enough for village fishing docks and a small wharf for the provisioning boats that run up to the city when the road is slow. The smells are cooked grain from the brewery on one side of the square and hot iron from Ciar's forge on the other, at all hours, mixed with the weedy smell off the lake.

Vanguarders are Trefganner stock in a register that even Brenmath finds slightly intense. Proud, hardy, suspicious in a way that has been earned three times over, and bound to Brenmath by blood and obligation to a degree that makes the two-day gap in the road feel more like a commute than a distance. A Vanguarder girl who marries into the city is still a Vanguarder. A Brenmath man who marries in is a Vanguarder within a year or he leaves. The hostility to strangers is the scrutiny a parent gives an unknown adult walking up to their child, and it relaxes the moment a traveler can prove no Remosan connection. Locals will answer your questions truthfully and watch your hands while they do it. After three days they will start to be friendly. After a week they will tell you war stories. Toward anyone of Remosan descent the watching never relaxes, regardless of how many decades pass.
The wait

The peacetime life of the village is provisioning. Grain and vegetables from the fields, apples from the orchards, ironwork from the forge, beer from the brewery, and the steady minor trade that has accumulated around the village over the centuries. Carts leave for Brenmath every third morning and come back two days later with whatever the city has sent down in return. On market days the square is crowded, the forge is loud, and children run in the lanes the way children run anywhere.

The chapel bell does not tell time. It rings once a year on the anniversary of the Third March, and otherwise has only one meaning. Every adult in Vanguard has trained for the moment it rings outside of spring, and most of them check the bell rope in passing without thinking about it. The orchard paths, the connected cellars under the houses, the three ways out of the square in the dark: these are things the village knows and does not discuss.
The Forge

Ciar Ni Hemmarth came to Brenmath on a Haldrith guild commission thirty-odd years ago, finished the work in eight years, stayed in the city for another eight, and then walked two days south on the Quiet Road to find somewhere he could work in peace. The villagers tolerated him fast because his work is undeniable and because a Haldrith dwarf with no Remosan connection is exactly the kind of outsider Vanguard can stomach. He has been here for most of three decades and considers himself a local. The villagers consider him a local with caveats.

His apprentice is Cliona, a gnome wizard of some seventy years' service, who decided early that she would never find a more fitting specimen to learn from than Ciar and has been enchanting his work ever since. She is very good. A blade she has finished can hold an edge no whetstone would produce, shed blood without dulling, and do things in a hand that are not written down anywhere. The prices reflect it. The wait list is currently about two years for anything more ambitious than a well-made kitchen knife, and the clients who can afford that wait include Brenmath's Warons, a handful of private buyers up and down the Quiet Road, and the occasional Synod functionary who has learned to pay out of pocket because the city will not approve the expense. Ciar and Cliona insist they are not a couple. She cooks his meals, lives in his house, and finishes his sentences. The village has stopped pretending to believe them.

That the best smithing operation in Trefgann is housed in Vanguard is not an accident. A village that has served as the staging ground for every invasion in living memory attracts a craftsman whose work is bought up at every muster, and Ciar's forge has outfitted Vanguard's council and much of Brenmath's senior militia for three decades running. Ciar did not come here for this reason. He came for the quiet. The village recognized what his presence meant inside a season.
The Brewery

Valor Brewery is the village's other pride and its largest building, a squat stone hall at the south end of the square that smells of cooked grain and hops at all hours. Valor brews corn and buckwheat beer, which is what the local soil gives, and the standard comparison up and down the Quiet Road is that Valor is as good as beer gets on this side of the water. Most inns between the Southfield border and Brenmath carry at least one Valor cask, and the ones that do not are either trying to pass off a cheaper substitute or have annoyed the brewery enough to lose their allocation. Old Vassik runs the place, eighty-something and a child of the Third March, small and mean and personally known to every innkeeper on the road.

The brewery is also the closest thing Vanguard has to a civic building. Weddings are held in the yard. Harvest dinners happen in the mash room after the vessels have been cleaned. The back room is where a council of four militia veterans meets when there is something to decide and ignores each other when there is not. The council has no formal authority and is universally obeyed. Its current senior member is Karsa Halric, sixty-eight, who fought in the Third March as a teenager and has been on the council for twenty years. She is the woman strangers are warned about by anyone friendly enough to warn them. The council coordinates the muster, settles property disputes, and decides which travelers are allowed to stay at the Etched Spear.

Vassik is not on the council and has not been invited. He is, however, in the next room during every meeting, and the council does not bother closing the door. This has made him the quiet fifth member of every decision the village has made in the last forty years without his name appearing on anything. He has not bought a bottle of Eoghan's wine in fifty years and has no plans to start.
Notable Locations
The Etched Spear:

The inn for outsiders, run by Eoghan, a half-elf who fought on the Remosan side in the Third March and deserted at the end of it to find a quiet life in Trefgann. Inside is a composition of low tables, mismatched pillows, and patched chairs arranged in an order that only makes sense once you have sat in it for ten minutes. He serves tea, wine, and vegetable dishes from the walled garden behind the building, without apology for any of them. A single Remosan grape vine grows against the garden wall and produces enough fruit for two bottles of wine a year. He prunes it obsessively. Nobody in the village has ever asked about it.
The Standing Mug:

The locals' drinking house, an unmarked door on a side street off the square, run as a side concern by the brewery. Strangers are not refused entry. They are simply not poured a drink, and most figure out what is happening within fifteen minutes and leave.
Ciar's Forge:

A stone-built workshop near the lakeside docks with a chimney that smokes most of the day. Ciar works at the main anvil. Cliona has a smaller workbench by the window where the light is better for the inscriptions, surrounded by jars of things the villagers do not know the names of and do not want to. Commissions taken in person, on a two-year wait, at prices set the day of.
Valor Brewery:

The squat stone hall at the south end of the square, smelling of grain and hops at all hours. Visitors can buy a cask at the front door if they have a cart to haul it and if Vassik is in a mood to sell, which he usually is. The yard holds weddings, the mash room holds harvest dinners, and the back room holds the council.
The Marker Stone:

A low stone in the center of the square, carved with three dates. No inscription explains them. Villagers passing it will sometimes touch the stone on the way somewhere else, and its corners are worn smooth.
The Chapel:

A small stone chapel on the east side of the square, plain inside and lightly used. The bell in the low tower rings once a year on the spring anniversary and otherwise only for one reason. Father Ossir, the aging cleric, keeps the chapel's records in a locked chest and has not opened it in six years.
Plot Hooks
The Bell:

Two months ago the chapel bell rang for about fifteen seconds, outside any anniversary, and nobody has admitted to ringing it. Nobody in the village has discussed it openly since. The runners' horses have been kept fresh for eight weeks. Karsa Halric has been checking the western horizon at dawn for the same eight weeks. The question of who rang it and why is not being asked, because asking it out loud is the same as saying out loud that something is coming, and nobody wants to be the first to do that. The party arrives in a village that is not quite admitting it is on a war footing.
The Commission:

A Synod functionary from a northern city commissioned a pair of ceremonial blades from Ciar two years ago, paid up front in good coin, and is arriving to collect them in twelve days. Ciar finished the blades a month ago. Cliona has not finished the enchantments, will not say why, and will not let Ciar near them. Ciar has stopped sleeping. The functionary is not a patient man, and the village does not know which side of the argument they want to be on when he arrives.
The Traveler at the Spear:

Eoghan is hosting a young woman who says she is on a trading journey from the western country, and whose surname is unmistakably Remosan. She is eighteen years old and was born in Trefgann. Eoghan has seen her papers and believes her. The council has heard about her and is meeting on Thursday to decide whether to escort her out of the village at sundown or let her leave in her own time. Eoghan is refusing to evict her on his own, for the first time in fifty years, and Karsa Halric is furious that he is making her make the call.
